source: CIRCL CVE Search + GitHub Advisory OSV + CISA KEV + NIST NVD

cves.summary: The Ortto plugin for WordPress before 1.0.25 did not filter the WooCommerce product data it embedded in public storefront pages. An unauthenticated threat actor could read product passwords and private product metadata from an affected store.

The Ortto plugin for WordPress before 1.0.25 did not authenticate configuration update requests, relying only on a secret exposed in public HTML. An unauthenticated threat actor could overwrite the plugin's configuration to serve arbitrary scripts.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

sched_ext: Wait for SCX_OPSS_DISPATCHING before moving tasks off DSQs

A task can be found on a non-local DSQ while the CPU which dispatched it
is still running ops.dequeue() and hasn't cleared SCX_OPSS_DISPATCHING.
The DSQ consume and move paths don't wait for the dispatch to finish and
can operate on the task concurrently with the dispatcher.

Call scx_wait_dispatching() in scx_move_local_task_to_local_dsq(),
unlink_dsq_and_switch_rq_lock() and move_task_between_dsqs() before they
operate on the task. In scx_move_local_task_to_local_dsq(), wait before
scx_resolve_local_dsq() as it may update p->scx.flags.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

io_uring: wake ring pollers for local task_work

With IORING_SETUP_DEFER_TASKRUN completions are queued as local work, and
only become CQEs when the submitter enters the kernel to wait for events.
For an application that finds out via poll() or epoll on the ring fd when
it is time to do that, io_uring_poll() reports EPOLLIN if local work is
pending.

That only helps if the work is there at the time of the call. When
DEFER_TASKRUN was added, io_req_local_work_add() did io_cqring_wake(),
which took care of tasks sleeping in poll() as well. Then polling got a
wait queue of its own, ->poll_wq, and the wake up in
io_req_local_work_add() was replaced by waking the submitter directly.
Since then ->poll_wq is only woken when CQEs are committed, which for
such a ring is done by the very task that is waiting to be told to:

  submitter                           completion
  poll(ring_fd)
    io_uring_poll()  // nothing yet
    schedule()
                                      io_req_local_work_add()
                                        // ->cq_wait_nr: nobody waits
  // sleeps on

Wake ->poll_wq when the first entry is put on the work list. Like for the
eventfd, that must not be done right away if the work is queued from a
wake up handler, as the chain of wake ups could get back to the wait
queue whose lock is held. Use an RCU callback in that case, with a
reference to the ring.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

io_uring/napi: make stale entries time out after 60s

With dynamic tracking a NAPI id that hasn't been seen for a minute is
meant to be dropped from the list the ring busy polls. The timeout is
added to jiffies, but it is defined as 60 * SEC_CONVERSION, and
SEC_CONVERSION isn't the number of jiffies in a second. It is the
internal factor of __timespec64_to_jiffies(), HZ scaled up by
SEC_JIFFIE_SC bits. For HZ=1000 that is 1000 << 22, which puts the
timeout at about eight years. On 32-bit the multiplication overflows.

So entries are never removed, and every id that a socket of the ring
ever had keeps being polled on each wait.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

io_uring/net: don't retry recv on uncommitted buffers

Commit 41b70df5b38b ("io_uring/net: commit partial buffers on retry")
commits ring provided buffers when a receive is going to be retried after
a partial transfer, so that another request using the same buffer group
can't be handed the memory the first one keeps receiving into. It commits
the number of bytes received so far. That does the job for a single
buffer which is consumed as a whole, but the request hangs on to all it
has mapped:

- For a buffer ring with IOU_PBUF_RING_INC only these bytes are consumed.
  The rest of the buffer stays at the head of the ring.
- For a bundle only the buffers which hold these bytes are consumed, the
  others that were peeked stay in the ring.

In both cases the next receive with that buffer group gets memory that
the retried request is still going to write to, and whoever comes last
overwrites the data of the other. What the retry fills isn't committed at
all, as the buffer list isn't known any more at that point. So the kernel
hands it out again later on, while the CQE tells the application that it
was used, and for an incremental buffer that it is done with.

The remainder can't be committed in advance: if the request ends up
receiving less, there is no way to tell the application that more was
consumed than the CQE accounts for. Complete the request with what it has
got instead of retrying it. MSG_WAITALL is no longer honoured for
receives into incremental buffers or multi buffer bundles, they can
return a short count, with the request marked as failed like for other
short MSG_WAITALL transfers.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

soc/tegra: pmc: Fix uninitialised clock rate

For legacy 32-bit Tegra devices, the warning in the
tegra_pmc_enter_suspend_mode() function is being triggered because the
early_pmc->rate variable is never configured and hence, always 0. This
issue started occurring after updating the PMC driver to create the PMC
context dynamically which causes the 'rate' to be set in the new dynamic
context, but missed updating the rate in the early PMC context.

Fix this by initialising the early_pmc->rate variable for 32-bit Tegra
devices when the rate for the PMC context is initialised.

[treding@nvidia.com: move assignment to existing #ifdef block]

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

io_uring/poll: avoid retry wakeup loss when dropping ownership

If a wakeup sets IO_POLL_RETRY_FLAG between the owning task consuming
the existing instance of IO_POLL_RETRY_FLAG and the loop check
of io_poll_check_events(), then we stall on processing the request
until an unrelated wakeup comes along.

Using atomic_cmpxchg instead of atomic_sub_return to guarantee both the
count v and poll_refs are 0 and no wake-ups are missed.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

io_uring/openclose: keep the lock in io_pipe_fixed()

io_pipe_fixed() installs both ends of the pipe in the fixed file table,
drops ->uring_lock, and copies the slot numbers to the application. If
that faults, it takes the lock again and removes whatever is in these
slots.

If the request is run by io-wq the lock really is dropped in between, and
the slots are visible to everybody else. By the time the error path gets
to them, they may have been closed and reused, by IORING_OP_CLOSE and a
direct open or accept, or by IORING_REGISTER_FILES_UPDATE. Then a file is
removed from the table that has nothing to do with the failed request.

Do the copy with the lock held. Faulting in user memory under
->uring_lock is fine, the registration paths do it all the time.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/amdgpu: correct reservation fence slots for userq per-vm BOs eviction

It fixes both the move overflow and the eviction fence add for
evicting these per-vm BOs.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

io_uring/zcrx: fix buffer offsets in areas above 4GB

io_zcrx_queue_cqe() computes the offset of the buffer in its area from
net_iov_idx(), which is an unsigned int, so the shift is done in 32 bits
and only the result is widened to the u64 that goes into the CQE. An area
can be up to 1TB in size. For every niov beyond the first 4GB the CQE
points the application at a buffer 4GB, or a multiple of that, below the
one which has the data. It reads the wrong data, and then returns a
buffer it doesn't own via the refill queue while the real one is never
given back.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

io_uring/timeout: don't lose a cancel as io-wq arms a timeout

An IORING_OP_TIMEOUT run by io-wq, because of IOSQE_ASYNC, has the same
problem as poll, futex and waitid. io_wq_submit_work() looks at
IO_WQ_WORK_CANCEL once, before it issues the request. A cancel in between
flags the work, gets -EALREADY, and searches ->timeout_list in vain,
while the worker then adds the request and starts the timer:

  io-wq worker                          io_try_cancel()
  io_wq_submit_work()
    IO_WQ_WORK_CANCEL isn't set
                                        io_async_cancel_one()
                                          sets IO_WQ_WORK_CANCEL
                                          = -EALREADY
                                        io_timeout_cancel() = -ENOENT
    io_timeout()
      adds the request to ->timeout_list
      hrtimer_start()
    = IOU_ISSUE_SKIP_COMPLETE

Nobody looks at the flag again, and the timeout runs its course. At ring
exit, io_uring_try_cancel_requests() cancels io-wq work and then kills
the timeouts the same way, so an exiting task can get stuck for the full
duration of such a timeout.

Look at the flag under ->timeout_lock, which the search takes as well,
and fail the request if it is set. If the search came first, the flag is
visible. If it comes later, it finds the request on the list.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ntfs: fix resident conversion in ntfs_new_attr_flags

When setting sparse/compressed flags on a resident attribute, the
function skipped the resident-to-non-resident conversion and
terminated.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

io_uring/io-wq: don't hide a link from cancellations

A task that exits cancels its tracked requests and waits until they are
gone. io_uring_cancel_generic() looks everywhere a request can be, and
goes to sleep if it found nothing to cancel. It is woken up each time
one of the requests of the task is completed by task work or freed.

When io-wq is done with a request that has a link, there is a time in which
the next request of the link can't be found:

  io_worker_handle_work()
    io_assign_current_work(worker, NULL)
    io_wq_free_work(work)
      io_req_find_next()           // takes the link off the request
      io_free_req()                // task work for the task
    io_assign_current_work(worker, linked)
      io_run_task_work()
      cond_resched()
      worker->cur_work = linked

It is not pending, it is not the current work of a worker, and it is not
yet on the list that it is about to be parked on. If the pass that the
exiting task makes because of io_free_req() falls into that time, it finds
nothing and the task goes to sleep. The worker then runs the link, which
IO_WQ_BIT_EXIT doesn't prevent for bounded work. If that parks the request
nothing is completed or freed, and nobody wakes up the task. If it is the
process that exits it can't be killed any more either.

  NOP, IOSQE_ASYNC | IOSQE_IO_LINK
  FUTEX_WAIT, FUTEX2_PRIVATE
  exit of the thread, or of the process, up to 63us later

With four of these per round 5 to 8 of 10,000 rounds hang (4 CPUs, KVM):

  io_uring_cancel_generic
  do_exit

Commit f8b632e89a10 ("io_uring: tighten task exit cancellations") is about
the same gap, and makes the task look again for whatever happens before
io_free_req().

Free the request once the link is the current work of the worker, or
pending. Whoever is woken up by that can find the link, until it is parked
where cancellations look as well. To do so split io_wq_free_work() in two.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

io_uring/mpscq: disable preemption while pushing

A push makes the node the new tail, and then links it to its predecessor.
In between the queue isn't empty, but mpscq_pop() can't get at the node.
The consumers deal with that by trying again, with a cond_resched() in
the loop to give a preempted producer the chance to finish.

cond_resched() doesn't do that if the consumer has a higher priority than
the producer and both have to use the same CPU:

  producer (SCHED_OTHER)              consumer (SCHED_FIFO), same CPU
  io_req_local_work_add()
    mpscq_push()
      prev = xchg(&q->tail, node)
  <preempted>                         io_cqring_wait()
                                        __io_run_local_work()
                                      again:
                                          cond_resched()  // nothing to do
                                          mpscq_pop()     // NULL
                                          // work pending, no events yet
                                          goto again

The producer can be any task that is able to queue task_work for the
ring: an io-wq worker, or somebody who sends a message with
IORING_OP_MSG_RING. The consumer spins, holding ->uring_lock, until the
scheduler takes pity on the fair class, which takes about a second with
the default settings of the fair server, and forever without it. The
loops in tctx_task_work_run() and io_cancel_local_task_work() have the
same problem.

Don't allow preemption between the two steps. That bounds the time the
window is open on the CPU of the producer by what interrupts take, and a
consumer that waits for that is on another CPU. The cost is a
preempt_disable()/preempt_enable() pair per push.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

dm cache: fix issue with background work locking

dm cache used a rw_semaphore for background_work_lock. Write locks on
rw_semaphores have strict owner semantics, but there was no guarantee
that the process that locked background_work_lock was the same process
that unlocked it. This can be easily seen using a kernel compiled with
CONFIG_DEBUG_RWSEMS. Given a dm cache device <cache>, run: 'dmsetup
suspend <cache> && dmsetup resume <cache>'. This will trigger a kernel
warning:

DEBUG_RWSEMS_WARN_ON((rwsem_owner(sem) != current) && !rwsem_test_oflags(sem, RWSEM_NONSPINNABLE))

triggered by cache_resume(). To fix this, switch from a rw_semaphore to
a spinlock and a wait queue. dm cache already has a wait queue and
associated counter, migration_wait and nr_allocated_migrations, that was
getting woken up when background work was getting completed, but wasn't
actually used by anything. This is replaced by the background_work queue
and counter.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

Drivers: hv: Avoid infinite retry loop in init_vp_index()

There is a retry loop in init_vp_index() where the CPUs from a certain
node are stripped out if they have already been in the allocated cpumask
or not in HK_TYPE_MANAGED_IRQ housekeeping cpumask. If there is no
CPU left, the allocated cpumask is ignored and the process is retried
again. However, if the HK_TYPE_MANAGED_IRQ housekeeping cpumask turns
out not to contain any CPU in that particular node, that will become an
infinite retry loop.  This particular problem was reported by sashiko
[1]. This should rarely happen, but we still need to guard against this.

Fix this infinite loop problem by also skipping NUMA node that has no
housekeeping CPU in the inner while loop of init_vp_index(). Also update
the early abort check to check for the absence of online housekeeping
CPUs instead of just the emptiness of the cpumask. As the outer for
loop will only be reached if the housekeeping cpumask has at least one
online CPU, a NUMA node with housekeeping CPUs will eventually be found.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

pid_namespace: make zap_pid_ns_processes() freezable

When the init of a pid namespace exits, zap_pid_ns_processes() waits
until all other pids in the namespace are freed. A tracer outside the
namespace that does not reap its traced zombies keeps those pids
allocated, so this wait has no upper bound, and while it lasts every
suspend attempt fails:

  Freezing user space processes failed after 20.006 seconds (2 tasks refusing to freeze, wq_busy=0):

Neither wait is freezable. The first loop sleeps in do_wait(), which
returns -ERESTARTSYS on the freezer's fake signal; the loop then clears
TIF_SIGPENDING and waits again without ever freezing. The final loop
sleeps in TASK_INTERRUPTIBLE, and since nothing clears TIF_SIGPENDING
there, schedule() returns immediately after the first freeze attempt
and the task spins until the wait ends.

Sleep in TASK_INTERRUPTIBLE | TASK_FREEZABLE in do_wait(), so that the
freezer can freeze tasks waiting there directly, and in TASK_IDLE |
TASK_FREEZABLE in the final loop, like coredump_task_exit() does.

This was hit with Chromium-based browsers: crashpad ptrace-attaches the
threads of a crashed renderer, which is a pid namespace init, and does
not reap those killed during the dump.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

io_uring: don't flood a cancelling task with task_work

io_ring_exit_work() asks each task which has used the ring to remove its
tctx node, by task_work, and repeats that until the list is empty.
io_tctx_exit_cb() doesn't touch the node while the task is in
io_uring_cancel_generic(), which removes all the nodes at its end. So the
work item queues the callback again as soon as it has completed, for
nothing.

That is more than a waste of time. task_work_run() only returns when it
finds the list empty. If the rings are released from inside the
cancellation, because requests of other rings held the last references to
their files, up to 64 work items keep sending callbacks to the one task
which is running them. It never finds the list empty, never gets back to
the cancellation, the nodes stay, and so it goes on: a task with 60 pairs
of rings which poll each other ran 280000 callbacks in 5 seconds, 20
seconds after exit_group(). It ends when all the senders happen to be late
at the same time. Until then the task keeps a CPU and the work items busy.

An exiting task can't be killed meanwhile. execve() cancels the requests in
the same way, so a live task can get stuck there as well, for minutes. If
it takes more than five, the work items run into the
WARN_ON_ONCE(time_after(jiffies, timeout)) of io_ring_exit_work(). No
privilege is needed for any of this.

If the callback has met a task in cancellation, wait a little before it is
sent again. Nobody has to wake the work item up for that: either the node
is gone by then, or it is the turn of the next round.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

io_uring/cancel: rearm local work wake up before sleep

io_uring_try_cancel_requests() sets ->cq_wait_nr to 1 so that the next
io_req_local_work_add() wakes the cancelling task. The add that takes the
count to zero is the only one that wakes, later ones see a count <= 0 and
return. io_uring_cancel_generic() however only becomes
TASK_INTERRUPTIBLE much later, so the one wake up can be spent on a
running task. That is fine as long as the entry of that add is still
queued, as the io_local_work_pending() check then skips the sleep. It is
not if the add was delayed after queueing its entry:

CPU0 (submitter in exec or exit)      CPU1 (io_req_local_work_add)
                                      mpscq_push(req A)
io_uring_try_cancel_requests()
  io_run_local_work()  // runs req A
io_uring_try_cancel_requests()
  atomic_set(&ctx->cq_wait_nr, 1)
                                      atomic_read(&ctx->cq_wait_nr) == 1
                                      count taken, wake_up_state()
                                        // task is running, no-op
prepare_to_wait(TASK_INTERRUPTIBLE)
io_local_work_pending() == false
schedule()
                                      mpscq_push(req B)
                                      cq_wait_nr <= 0, return

Only the sleeping task can run req B, so it is stuck in execve() until a
signal happens to wake it. An exiting task doesn't even get that.

Arm the count again once the task state is set and before the work list
is checked, for the rings whose local work this task is the one to run.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

x86/hyperv: Avoid using per-cpu output page in hv_apicid_to_vp_index()

hv_apicid_to_vp_index() currently uses the per-cpu hypercall input
and output pages. This function is called when running in VTL2 and
when running in an SEV-SNP CoCo VM with no paravisor. In the former
case, the output page is allocated, but in the latter case it is
not, so the hypervisor stores the output VP index in memory that has
not been allocated by the guest.

Fix this by using the input page for both input and output. The
hypercall has very small input and output, so sharing the same
page for both is straightforward. An alternative fix is to
allocate the per-cpu output page when running in an SEV-SNP CoCo
guest, but this uses significantly more memory, particularly
with larger vCPUs counts.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

printk: Postpone kthread startup

There have been various bug reports related to SMP systems hanging
on boot. The reports vary but seem to have some overlap with regard
to missed IPI's during SMP setup. The reports also show that
reverting NBCON console usage allows the bugs to disappear.

The NBCON kthreads for console printing are started very early
during boot using early_initcall(). Since these kthreads are
asynchronously enabling/disabling interrupts during early boot, they
may be interfering with early SMP setup on some hardware platforms.

Starting the console printing kthreads later has shown to avoid the
hanging on systems that could previously reproduce the issue.

Postpone kthread starting until after all arch initcalls have
completed.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

gpio: shared: gracefully handle no-device lookup of shared GPIOs

We use platform lookup tables for shared GPIOs. This mechanism needs a
struct device to work so fwnode-based lookup with no device associated
currently causes a NULL-pointer deference.

Adding this functionality will require a larger rework and it has never
worked anyway so add a check that allows the kernel to gracefully handle
this situation with an error ahead of implementing that functionality as
a new feature.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

tipc: protect node reset trace dump with node lock

The tipc_node_reset_links trace event asks tipc_node_dump() to walk the
node's link entries. Unlike the other node events that request link data,
this event runs without the node lock.

This permits bearer teardown to free a link while the trace callback is
dumping it:

  CPU 0                                CPU 1
  trace_tipc_node_reset_links()
    tipc_node_dump()
      l = n->links[0].link
                                       tipc_node_write_lock()
                                       kfree(l)
                                       n->links[0].link = NULL
                                       tipc_node_write_unlock()
      tipc_link_dump(l)

tipc_link_dump() then dereferences the stale pointer. KASAN reported:

  BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in tipc_link_dump
  Read of size 4 by task poc/115
  Call Trace:
   tipc_link_dump+0x10cb/0x16b0
   tipc_node_dump+0x4bb/0x740
   trace_event_raw_event_tipc_node_class+0x258/0x360
   tipc_node_reset_links+0x14d/0x1a0
   tipc_rcv+0x13f5/0x3030
   tipc_udp_recv+0x4e3/0x670
  Allocated by task 0:
   tipc_link_create+0x1e1/0x1020
   tipc_node_check_dest+0x7d2/0x11a0
   tipc_disc_rcv+0xdbf/0x1430
  Freed by task 89:
   kfree+0x131/0x3c0
   tipc_node_link_down+0x267/0x4b0
   tipc_node_delete_links+0xec/0x160
   bearer_disable+0x107/0x260

Take the node write lock around the trace event. This serializes the
dump against tipc_node_link_down(delete=true), which frees the link
under the same write lock.

In Eclipse Mnestix Browser versions 1.2.0 up until but excluding 2.3.0 it was possible for an unauthenticated attacker to perform actions that are only allowed to be executed by an authorized Mnestix user, like changing the Infrastructure settings or calling the connected and authenticated Mnestix AAS Generator backend.

Apache HertzBeat versions 1.7.1, 1.7.2, 1.7.3, 1.8.0, and 1.9.0 have incomplete XPath expression validation in the HTTP collector XML parsing path. An authenticated user with permission to create monitor templates can supply XPath expressions through metrics.aliasFields that are evaluated without the validation applied to parseScript. When processing a crafted XML response, repeated evaluation may consume excessive CPU resources and impair collector availability. This is a follow-up to the incomplete fix for CVE-2026-24343. The fix is included in Apache HertzBeat 1.9.1. Users should upgrade to 1.9.1 or a later version.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KEYS: Fix key_reject_and_link() race with keyring restriction

The restrict_link check in key_reject_and_link() is done before taking
the keyring semaphore, racing with a concurrent keyring_restrict()
that installs the restriction while holding the semaphore in write
mode.

Move the check to after __key_link_lock(), so it is done under the
semaphore, matching the pattern used in __key_create_or_update().

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

io-wq: order the exit bit against worker creation task work

io_wq_exit_workers() cancels task work for queued worker creation with
task_work_cancel_match(). That has a plain load of task->task_works.

io_queue_worker_create() adds the new entry and tests IO_WQ_BIT_EXIT to
cancel it if the workqueue is already on its way out.

That must be ordered. task_work_add() has a full barrier via cmpxchg().
But io_wq_exit_start() sets the bit with set_bit() which doesn't have
any memory ordering.

So afaict, on weakly ordered architectures the exiting task may load
task_works before the store of the bit is visible. The other side tests
the bit before the store is visible as well. So the entry remains queued
with worker_refs and the exiting task waits on worker_done indefinitely.

If the task still has rings then io_uring_del_tctx_node() provides the
barrier via test_and_set_bit() in io_wq_set_exit_on_idle(). When it
has closed all rings though that barrier is gone.

Add the barrier after the set_bit().

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

tracing: Do not initialize tracefs work if tracing is disabled

If trace buffer allocation fails during early boot (e.g.  in
early_trace_init() -> allocate_trace_buffers()), tracing_disabled is
left set to 1 and the global trace array events list remains
uninitialized.

Later during boot, tracer_init_tracefs() (invoked via fs_initcall)
queues tracerfs_init_work asynchronously without checking if tracing was
disabled.  When tracer_init_tracefs_work_func() runs, it calls
event_trace_init() and init_tracer_tracefs(&global_trace, NULL)
unconditionally.  This leads to __find_event_file() dereferencing an
uninitialized tr->events list, causing an early boot NULL pointer
dereference Oops:

  BUG: Kernel NULL pointer dereference on read at 0x00000010
  Faulting instruction address: 0xc000000000485be0
  Oops: Kernel access of bad area, sig: 7 [#1]
  ...
  NIP [c000000000485be0] __find_event_file+0x70/0x3c0
  LR  [c000000000448874] init_tracer_tracefs+0x274/0xc80
  Call Trace:
   init_tracer_tracefs+0x274/0xc80
   tracer_init_tracefs_work_func+0x50/0x320
   process_one_work+0x1e8/0x5c0
   worker_thread+0x1dc/0x3d0
   kthread+0x194/0x1b0
   start_kernel_thread+0x14/0x18

Check tracing_disabled at the beginning of tracer_init_tracefs_work_func()
and return immediately if tracing is disabled or failed to initialize,
preventing the crash.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

i2c: xiic: restore non-managed runtime PM to fix clk WARN flood

The devres conversion replaced manual pm_runtime_enable()/disable() with
devm_pm_runtime_set_active_enabled() and dropped the remove-time runtime
PM teardown. The managed release tears runtime PM down in the wrong
order: it calls pm_runtime_dont_use_autosuspend() before
pm_runtime_disable(), i.e. while runtime PM is still enabled, and devres
is LIFO so the devm_clk_get_enabled() release runs afterwards.

At remove(), pm_runtime_put_sync() leaves the device active with the
autosuspend timer armed. Clearing use_autosuspend then makes rpm_idle()
suspend immediately, and xiic_i2c_runtime_suspend() clk_disable()s the
clock. The later devm_clk_get_enabled() release clk_disable_unprepare()s
the already-disabled clock, so clk_core_disable() WARNs ("clkN already
disabled") on every teardown.

Drop the managed helper and restore the non-managed runtime PM setup and
teardown, so runtime PM is enabled once in probe and disabled once in
remove and the clock enable count stays balanced.

Order the remove teardown so runtime PM is disabled before the usage
count is dropped: pm_runtime_disable() followed by pm_runtime_put_noidle()
instead of pm_runtime_put_sync(). Dropping the count first with autosuspend
still enabled arms the autosuspend timer, and a preemption before
pm_runtime_disable() lets it expire, suspend the device and clk_disable()
the clock, which the devm release then disables again - the same WARN.

Restore the non-managed IRQ request as well. The probe error paths now
unwind runtime PM by hand via goto, and a devm-registered handler is only
freed later during devres unwind, so it would stay live across the manual
teardown (and across any future failing step added after it). Request the
IRQ with request_threaded_irq() and free it explicitly in the probe error
path and in remove. The probe error path also clears use_autosuspend, to
match the teardown in remove().

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

pid_namespace: prevent TIF_NOTIFY_SIGNAL from interrupting the reaper

Since commit 7fea700e04bd ("zap_pid_ns_processes: clear
TIF_NOTIFY_SIGNAL along with TIF_SIGPENDING") zap_pid_ns_processes()
clears TIF_NOTIFY_SIGNAL before every kernel_wait4() call. Otherwise
kernel_wait4() doesn't sleep and returns -ERESTARTSYS if
signal_pending() is true and the reaper busy-waits.

But clearing TIF_NOTIFY_SIGNAL doesn't fix it. It can get raised again.
For example, klp_send_signals() sets it raw against any task that hasn't
transitioned yet. And it keeps sending it until the livepatch finishes.

The sleep loop waiting for pid_allocated to drop has the same problem
and it doesn't even clear anything. So a schedule() in
TASK_INTERRUPTIBLE returns immediately.

Use a no_notify_signal guard. signal_pending() will ignore
TIF_NOTIFY_SIGNAL and the pid namespace reaper sleeps until a child
exits or free_pid() wakes it.
ZohoCorp ManageEngine Key Manager Plus versions before 7151 allow authenticated users to enter malicious input when configuring a Microsoft CA
ZohoCorp ManageEngine Key Manager Plus versions up to 7150 allow authenticated users to export certificates belonging to other users to their own registered key vaults.

Content of external URL mails, their stylesheets and images to embed is fetched by the server without validating the target host. Backend users with access to the mail module can make the server send requests to hosts in the internal network.
In Eclipse Mnestix Browser versions 1.6.0 up until but excluding 2.3.0 it was possible for an unauthenticated attacker to exfiltrate the MNESTIX_BACKEND_API_KEY for all configured Infrastructures.
ManageEngine Key Manager Plus versions before 7151 are vulnerable to an improper access control issue that allow authenticated users to modify another user's ACME certificate deployment credentials.

The actions linked in the emails of the extension (e.g. to confirm a registration or the deletion of an account) do not reject requests with a missing or invalid hash. Instead, the frontend user given in the request is used. Unauthenticated attackers can therefore perform these actions for arbitrary active frontend users. This allows them to retrieve the email address or username of all frontend users and to delete arbitrary frontend user accounts.

Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal') in the ShareActivity component of BlueLM Copilot (com.vivo.ai.copilot) allows a malicious application installed on the same device to write arbitrary files via a crafted ACTION_SEND intent with a ContentProvider-supplied file name containing '..' sequences.

Backend actions and ajax routes of the mail module do not check whether the backend user has access to the page of the requested mail or recipient group. Backend users with access to the mail module can view, change, send and export mails and recipient groups outside their web mounts, including the personal data of recipients.

The HTML content of mails and tracked URLs are rendered unescaped in the backend module. Backend users with access to the mail module can inject arbitrary HTML and JavaScript, which is executed in the context of other backend users viewing the mail preview or report.

Płatnik performs client-side authentication. An attacker with access to any application instance connected to the backend server can bypass the login verification process and authenticate as an arbitrary user.

This issue was fixed in metric 242 in version 10.02.002.

Use of a weak password encoding algorithm in Płatnik software allows a user who obtains encoded password to easily decode it. 

This issue was fixed in metric 242 in version 10.02.002.

A flaw was found in GStreamer's gst-plugins-good package. The FLV media demuxer does not properly validate buffer sizes and data availability when processing enhanced audio and video tags in malformed or truncated FLV streams. A remote attacker could exploit this vulnerability by providing a specially crafted FLV media file that, when opened or streamed by a GStreamer-based application, triggers an assertion failure or a process crash, leading to denial of service.

** UNSUPPORTED WHEN ASSIGNED ** Improper restriction of recursive entity references in DTDs ('XML entity expansion') vulnerability in Apache JClouds.

This issue affects Apache JClouds: all versions.

As this project is retired, we do not plan to release a version that fixes this issue. Users are recommended to find an alternative or restrict access to the instance to trusted users.

NOTE: This vulnerability only affects products that are no longer supported by the maintainer.

** UNSUPPORTED WHEN ASSIGNED ** Improper input validation vulnerability in Apache Oozie. An authenticated Oozie user can reconfigure another tenant's
workflow job and change its ownership.

This issue affects Apache Oozie: all versions.

As this project is retired, we do not plan to release a version that fixes this issue. Users are recommended to find an alternative or restrict access to the instance to trusted users.

NOTE: This vulnerability only affects products that are no longer supported by the maintainer.

Saving the configuration of the mail backend module writes submitted settings to the page TSconfig without restricting them to the configuration options of the module. Backend users with access to the mail module can write arbitrary page TSconfig.

The click tracking middleware does not validate the authentication code of a recipient if the code is omitted. Unauthenticated attackers can retrieve personal data of newsletter recipients, which is inserted into links of sent mails.
The click tracking middleware accepts an arbitrary target URL and redirects to it. Attackers can misuse links to the website to redirect users to external sites.

Płatnik uses HTTP protocol to download updates, libraries and support files. It allows an attacker to conduct a Man-In-The-Middle attack, obtain transmitted data and replace the original files with their own.

This issue was fixed in metric 242 in version 10.02.002.

A flaw was found in uv. This vulnerability allows an attacker to execute malicious code during package resolution or installation via specially crafted ZIP (Zipped Information Package) archives that exploit parsing differentials, requiring user interaction to install an attacker-controlled package.
